title: Christian Apologetics
summary: Giving reasons for the hope within us: evidence for God, the reliability of the Bible, the resurrection of Jesus, and answers to common objections, shared with gentleness and respect.
description: Apologetics is the defence of the Christian faith. This course explains the biblical basis and right spirit of apologetics, the main arguments for God's existence, the reliability of the Bible, the historical evidence for the resurrection of Jesus, and answers to hard questions about suffering, science, other religions and the claim that Christianity is a foreign religion. It is designed for students, workers and church leaders who meet doubters and sceptics.
objectives: Explain the biblical basis and spirit of apologetics
Present reasonable arguments for the existence of God
Present the evidence for the resurrection of Christ
Answer common objections with gentleness and respect
outcomes: Explain 1 Peter 3:15 and Paul's approach in Athens
Summarise the cosmological, design and moral arguments
Explain manuscript evidence and the canon
Present the minimal facts for the resurrection
Respond to the problem of evil and the 'foreign religion' objection

modules.title: Why and How We Defend the Faith
modules.intro: Apologetics is commanded in Scripture and must be done in Christ's spirit. This week we lay the foundation.

lessons.title: Ready to give an answer
lessons.body:
"But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear" (1 Peter 3:15). The word *answer* is the Greek *apologia*, a reasoned defence.

Paul was "set for the defence of the gospel" (Philippians 1:17). He "reasoned" in synagogues and the marketplace (Acts 17:2, 17). Jude urged believers to "earnestly contend for the faith" (Jude 3).

Apologetics strengthens believers' confidence, removes obstacles for seekers, and answers attacks on the truth. It does not replace the Spirit or the gospel, but clears the way for them.

lessons.title: Faith and reason
lessons.body:
Biblical faith is not blind belief against evidence. It is trust in a God who has acted in history. Luke wrote "that thou mightest know the certainty of those things" (Luke 1:4). Jesus "shewed himself alive after his passion by many infallible proofs" (Acts 1:3). John wrote his signs "that ye might believe" (John 20:31).

Yet reason alone cannot save. Sin affects the mind (Romans 1:21; 2 Corinthians 4:4), and the Spirit must open eyes (1 Corinthians 2:14).

So we use reason humbly as a servant of faith, trusting God to work through truth, prayer and the gospel.

lessons.title: The right spirit
lessons.body:
Apologetics must be done "with meekness and fear" (1 Peter 3:15), not with arrogance or anger. "The servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves" (2 Timothy 2:24-25).

Paul in Athens listened, observed their culture, found common ground (their altar "TO THE UNKNOWN GOD"), quoted their poets, and then proclaimed Christ and the resurrection (Acts 17:22-31).

Aim to win people, not arguments. Listen to the question behind the question; sometimes a hard question comes from personal pain. And live in a way that matches the truth (1 Peter 3:16).

modules.title: Does God Exist?
modules.intro: This week we study classic arguments that point to God's existence.

lessons.title: The cosmological argument
lessons.body:
Everything that begins to exist has a cause. The universe began to exist, as both Scripture ("In the beginning God created", Genesis 1:1) and modern cosmology suggest. Therefore the universe has a cause.

That cause must be beyond space, time and matter, immensely powerful and personal (able to choose to create). This fits the God of the Bible: "Through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear" (Hebrews 11:3).

The question "Who made God?" misunderstands: God did not begin to exist. He is eternal (Psalm 90:2).

lessons.title: The design argument
lessons.body:
"The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork" (Psalm 19:1). Paul says God's "eternal power and Godhead" are "clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made" (Romans 1:20).

The universe shows remarkable order: physical constants finely tuned for life, the complex information in DNA, the intricate design of the eye and the cell. Just as a phone implies a designer, such complexity points to a Designer.

Some answer that chance and natural processes explain everything. Christians respond that natural laws themselves need explanation, and that information and fine-tuning are best explained by intelligence.

lessons.title: The moral argument
lessons.body:
Almost everyone believes some things are truly wrong: torturing children for fun, ritual killing, slavery. But if there is no God, right and wrong are only opinions or survival instincts. Why then should anyone be obliged to obey them?

Objective moral values point to a moral Lawgiver. Paul says the Gentiles "shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness" (Romans 2:15).

Africans widely share a sense of a Supreme Being and of moral order. These are pointers to the true God, who is fully revealed in Jesus Christ (John 1:18). Arguments do not save, but they show that faith is reasonable.

modules.title: The Bible and the Resurrection
modules.intro: Christianity stands or falls on the resurrection, recorded in a reliable Bible. This week we study the evidence.

lessons.title: Is the Bible reliable?
lessons.body:
Some claim the Bible has been changed. The evidence shows otherwise:

- **Manuscripts**: there are thousands of Greek manuscripts of the New Testament, some within a few generations of the originals, far more than for any other ancient book.
- **The Dead Sea Scrolls** (found 1947) include Old Testament texts about a thousand years older than previous copies, and show careful transmission.
- **Archaeology** has confirmed many places, rulers and customs mentioned in Scripture.
- **Eyewitnesses**: the Gospels come from eyewitnesses and their associates (2 Peter 1:16; 1 John 1:1-3).

Minor copying differences exist, but none affects any core doctrine. "The word of the Lord endureth for ever" (1 Peter 1:25).

lessons.title: The evidence for the resurrection
lessons.body:
Paul says, "if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain" (1 Corinthians 15:14). Facts widely accepted even by many sceptical historians include:

1. Jesus died by crucifixion.
2. His tomb was found empty, first by women (whose testimony was not valued then, so unlikely to be invented).
3. Many people, individually and in groups, believed they saw Him alive (1 Corinthians 15:5-8 lists over five hundred).
4. The disciples were transformed from fearful men into bold witnesses willing to die.
5. Sceptics such as James, Jesus' brother, and Paul, a persecutor, were converted.

The best explanation of these facts is that Jesus truly rose.

lessons.title: Alternative theories
lessons.body:
Other explanations fail:

- **The disciples stole the body** (Matthew 28:13): would they die for what they knew was a lie?
- **Jesus only fainted**: Roman executioners were experts; a half-dead man could not inspire belief in a glorious resurrection.
- **Hallucinations**: hallucinations are individual, not shared by groups of five hundred, and would not empty a tomb.
- **Wrong tomb**: the authorities could simply have produced the body.
- **Legend**: the resurrection was proclaimed in Jerusalem within weeks, while witnesses were alive (1 Corinthians 15:6).

The resurrection proves Jesus is the Son of God (Romans 1:4) and guarantees judgment (Acts 17:31).

modules.title: Hard Questions
modules.intro: This week we answer common hard questions about suffering, science, other religions and Christianity in Africa.

lessons.title: Why does God allow suffering?
lessons.body:
This is the hardest question. A full answer is beyond us, but Scripture gives light:

- Suffering entered through **sin and the fall** (Genesis 3; Romans 8:20-22), not through God's design for creation.
- God gave humans **real freedom**, and much suffering comes from human evil.
- God can bring **good out of evil**: Joseph said, "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good" (Genesis 50:20).
- God **suffered with us** in Christ, who wept and was crucified.
- God will **end all suffering** (Revelation 21:4) and judge all evil.

When someone asks in pain, comfort before you argue (Job 2:13).

lessons.title: Science and other religions
lessons.body:
**Science**: Many founders of modern science, such as Kepler, Newton and Faraday, were believers who saw science as "thinking God's thoughts after him". Science explains how the natural world works; it cannot explain why there is a world at all, or answer questions of meaning and morality. Christians differ on how to read the days of Genesis, but all affirm God as Creator.

**Other religions**: Religions contain some truth through general revelation, but they differ fundamentally on God, sin and salvation. Jesus' claim is unique: "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me" (John 14:6). Only Christianity offers salvation as a free gift through a God who became man, died and rose.

lessons.title: Is Christianity a foreign religion?
lessons.body:
Some say Christianity is the 'white man's religion' brought to colonise Africa. History says otherwise:

- Christianity began in the Middle East, not Europe, and Jesus lived in Asia, sheltered in Africa as a child (Matthew 2:13).
- Africans were among the first believers: the Ethiopian official (Acts 8), Simon of Cyrene, Lucius of Cyrene and Simeon Niger (Acts 13:1).
- North Africa produced great early theologians like Tertullian, Athanasius and Augustine, and Ethiopia has been Christian for over 1,600 years.
- In Nigeria, African agents like Samuel Ajayi Crowther did much of the missionary work.

The gospel belongs to every nation (Revelation 7:9), and Christ is Lord of all cultures.

short.q: What is apologetics and what spirit should mark it?
short.model: Apologetics is the reasoned defence of the faith (1 Peter 3:15), given with meekness, gentleness and respect.
Whatever begins to exist has a cause; the universe began; so it has a cause beyond space and time, which fits the eternal God.
Objective moral values exist; without God they would be mere opinion; so they point to a moral Lawgiver, as conscience witnesses (Romans 2:15).

short.q: Give three reasons to trust the reliability of the Bible.
short.model: Thousands of early manuscripts, the Dead Sea Scrolls showing careful transmission, and archaeological and eyewitness support.

short.q: List the main facts supporting the resurrection.
short.model: Jesus died by crucifixion, the tomb was empty, many saw Him alive, the disciples were transformed and sceptics like James and Paul were converted.

short.q: How would you answer the claim that Christianity is a foreign religion?
short.model: Christianity began in the Middle East, Africans were among its first believers (the Ethiopian, Simon of Cyrene), North Africa produced great early theologians, and Africans like Crowther led missions in Nigeria.
